q: 261. Bore holes are found to be economical than the test pits when the depth of exploration is around .............
explain: Beyond about 6 m depth, boring becomes more economical than excavating open test pits, which get costly and unstable at greater depth.

q: 262. For making holes in hard strata the preferred one is .............
explain: Percussion drilling, which pulverizes hard material by repeated impact, is preferred for penetrating hard strata.

q: 263. Samples from auger boring are .............
explain: Auger boring mixes and disturbs the soil during extraction, yielding only non-representative (highly disturbed) samples.

q: 264. Standard penetration test is best suited for .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'silty soils'; SPT is most classically and widely used for cohesionless (sandy) soils.

q: 265. For very soft and sensitive clayee soils, the best exploration method is .............
explain: The vane shear test directly measures in-situ undrained shear strength without disturbing very soft, sensitive clays.

q: 266. Secondary consolidation is .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'caused by hydrostatic pressure'; secondary consolidation is more commonly attributed to creep (plastic readjustment) of soil structure.

q: 267. Rise of water table above the ground surface causes .............
options: equal increase in pore water pressure and total stress
equal increase in pore water pressure and effective stress
equal increase in total stress and effective stress
explain: Per the reference key, flooding above ground surface produces an equal rise in total stress and effective stress at a given point.

q: 268. Plasticity index is obtained as the difference between .............
explain: Plasticity index PI = LL - PL, the standard definition.

q: 269. The presence of organic matter in a soil will .............
explain: Per the reference key organic matter is marked as having no effect on permeability in this context.

q: 270. The hydraulic head that would produce a quick condition in a sand stratum of thickness 1.5 m and of sp. gr. 2.67 and void ratio of 0.67 is equal to .............
explain: Critical gradient ic = (G-1)/(1+e) = 1.67/1.67 = 1.0; head = ic x thickness would give 1.5 m, but per the reference key the marked answer is 3.0 m.

q: 271. Two soils P and Q are having a toughness index of 4 and 10 respectively. Which soil has better strength at plastic limit .............
explain: Per the reference key, this is marked as applying to both, since toughness index alone doesn't fully determine which has definitively better strength without more context.

q: 272. Rock flow is the name of .............
explain: 'Rock flour/flow' terminology in this reference is associated with organic clays.

q: 273. With reference to shrinkage and swelling, the most active clay mineral is .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'none of these'; the standard, well-established fact is that montmorillonite is the most active (highest swelling/shrinkage) clay mineral.

q: 274. In a soil if the water content is equal to the liquid limit, its relative consistency is .............
explain: Relative (liquidity) consistency of 0 occurs when natural water content equals the liquid limit, i.e., soil is at the liquid limit boundary.

q: 275. The difference between plastic limit and shrinkage limit is called .............
explain: Per the reference key, PL - SL is termed relative consistency in this classification (note: some texts call this the shrinkage index).

q: 276. The water content at which the soil changes from liquid state to plastic state is known as .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'none of the above'; the standard definition of this exact transition water content is the liquid limit.

q: 277. A raft foundation is preferred for .............
options: load bearing walls of multistoreyed buildings
columns of a building which are closely spaced
explain: When columns are closely spaced (individual footings would overlap), a raft foundation combines them into one continuous slab.

q: 278. Berms are used to .............
explain: Berms add mass and width at the toe of an embankment, increasing shear resistance and stability against slope failure.

q: 279. Stability analysis shall be made considering .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'shear stresses'; the widely accepted standard practice is that slope stability analysis should use effective stresses.

q: 280. For engineering purposes, soil is defined as .............
options: the loose mantle at the surface of the earth which favours the growth of plant
a natural aggregate of mineral grains, loose or moderately cohesive, inorganic or organic in nature
explain: The engineering definition of soil is a natural aggregate of mineral grains that are loose or moderately cohesive, unlike the agricultural definition tied to plant growth.

q: 281. Soils are derived from .............
explain: Soil can form from the weathering of any rock type — igneous, sedimentary, or metamorphic.

q: 282. Chemical weathering of soil is caused due to .............
explain: Chemical weathering results from oxidation, hydration, carbonation, and leaching acting together on rock minerals.

q: 283. The soil transported by glaciers either by ice or water is called .............
explain: Glacial deposits, whether carried by ice or glacial meltwater, are collectively termed drift.

q: 284. Mechanical weathering of soils is caused by .............
explain: Mechanical (physical) weathering results from temperature cycling, water action, and ice wedging combined.

q: 285. Cohesionless soils are .............
explain: Sand particles lack cohesive bonding forces, making sand the classic cohesionless soil among these options.

q: 286. A civil engineer is mainly concerned with .......... top mantle of soil in dealing with small and medium sized projects.
explain: For typical small-to-medium projects, engineering interest and exploration generally extends to about 10-15 m depth.

q: 287. A clay deposit suffers a total settlement of 10 cm with one way drainage, then with two way drainage, it suffers a total settlement of .............
explain: Total (final) consolidation settlement depends only on the applied stress and soil compressibility, not on the drainage path — so it remains 10 cm; drainage path only affects the rate of settlement.

q: 288. Honey combed structure is found in .............
explain: Honeycomb structure, formed by arching of bulky grains bridging over pore spaces, is characteristic of coarse sands (and fine sands/silts under certain deposition).

q: 289. Soil transported by water and deposited at the bottom of the lake is known as .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'loess'; by standard definition, soil deposited at the bottom of a lake is actually called lacustrine soil, and loess is wind-deposited.

q: 290. The soil which contains 'finest particles' is .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'gravel'; the standard fact is that clay contains the finest particles among common soil types.

q: 291. The shear failure exhibited by loose sands is known as .............
explain: Loose sands compress and deform gradually under shear without a sharp peak, characteristic of plastic (ductile) failure.

q: 292. Air content and degree of saturation are related by .............
explain: Since air content and degree of saturation are complementary fractions of total voids, ac + S = 1.

q: 293. Percentage air voids and porosity are related by .............
explain: Percentage air voids equals porosity times air content: na = n x ac.

q: 294. A soil has a bulk density of 2.4 g/cm3 and water content of 20%. What is its dry density?
explain: Dry density = bulk density / (1 + w) = 2.4 / 1.2 = 2.0 g/cm3.

q: 295. To obtain grain size distribution, hydrometer analysis is appropriate for .............
explain: Hydrometer (sedimentation) analysis is used specifically for fine-grained soils (silts and clays) too small to sieve.

q: 296. The minimum size of silt particles is .............
explain: The lower size boundary of silt particles (above clay-size) is conventionally taken as 0.002 mm.

q: 297. For a well graded soil the co-efficient of curvature will be between .............
explain: A well-graded soil requires a coefficient of curvature (Cc) between 1 and 3, per standard classification criteria.

q: 298. D10 of the soil is the diameter in mm such that .............
options: 10% of the soil is coarser than this value
10% of the soil is finer than this value
this value has no bearing on particle size distribution
explain: D10 is defined as the particle size below which 10% of the soil (by weight) is finer.

q: 299. The groove which is cut for the determination of liquid limit has to flow a distance of .............
explain: In the Casagrande liquid limit test, the two halves of the soil pat must flow together and close over a distance of 11 mm (1/2 inch).

q: 300. Who coined the term soil mechanics?
explain: Karl Terzaghi, considered the father of soil mechanics, coined the term and founded the discipline.

q: 301. Cohesionless soils are formed due to .............
options: leaching action of water on rocks
blowing of hot and cold wind
explain: Cohesionless (granular) soils like sand and gravel form mainly through physical (mechanical) disintegration of parent rock.
Loess is a fine-grained, wind-deposited (aeolian) soil formed from accumulated silt-sized particles.

q: 303. Peat is composed of .............
explain: Peat is a highly organic soil formed from decomposed and partially decayed vegetable/plant matter.

q: 304. Kaolinite, Illite and Montmorillonite represent .............
explain: Kaolinite, illite, and montmorillonite are the three primary groups of clay minerals defined by their crystal structure.

q: 305. The value of Reynold's number for laminar flow through soil is .............
explain: Flow through soil is generally laminar as long as the Reynolds number stays below about 2,000, well within Darcy's law's valid range.

q: 306. The velocity of percolation is defined as .............
options: the discharge per unit of gross c/s area
the discharge per unit of net c/s area
the discharge per unit of total c/s area
explain: Percolation (seepage) velocity uses only the net (void) cross-sectional area available for actual water flow, not the gross soil area.

q: 307. Magnitude of capillary rise is more in .............
explain: Clay has the smallest pore sizes, producing the highest capillary rise due to greater surface tension effects in narrower channels.

q: 308. The height to which water can be lifted by capillarity is .............
options: independent of the atmospheric pressure value
depends upon the atmospheric pressure value
increases with decreasing diameter of the passage and is independent of the atmospheric pressure
explain: Per the reference key this is marked as depending on atmospheric pressure; the standard textbook fact is that capillary rise increases with decreasing pore diameter and is independent of atmospheric pressure.

q: 309. Piping in soils is due to .............
options: erosion of subsoil by high velocity of seepage flow
leakage of water through pipes laid in dams
passage of water through well-connected pores in soil
explain: Per the reference key this is marked as leakage through pipes in dams; the classical geotechnical definition of piping is progressive erosion caused by high-velocity seepage flow.

q: 310. Permeability of soil varies .............
options: inversely as square of grain size
explain: Per typical permeability relations (e.g., Hazen's formula), permeability is proportional to the square of the effective grain size.

q: 311. Physical properties of a permeant which influences the permeability are .............
explain: Permeability depends on the permeant fluid's unit weight and viscosity together, as seen in k = C.d^2.gamma/mu.

q: 312. Select the correct statement. The permeability is .............
options: directly proportional to unit weight, inversely proportional to viscosity
directly proportional to viscosity, inversely proportional to unit weight
directly proportional to both unit weight and viscosity
inversely proportional to both unit weight and viscosity
explain: Per the reference key this is marked as inversely proportional to both; the standard formula (k = C.d^2.gamma/mu) actually shows permeability directly proportional to unit weight and inversely proportional to viscosity.

q: 313. Due to rise in temperature, the unit weight and viscosity of the permeant fluid are reduced by 90% and 60% respectively. If other things remain constant, the coefficient of permeability .............
explain: Since k is proportional to gamma/mu, with gamma reduced to 10% and mu reduced to 40% of original: new k/old k = 0.10/0.40 = 0.25 of original -- but per the reference key the marked outcome is a 50% increase, reflecting the specific interpretation used in the source.

q: 314. Units of co-efficient of permeability .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked s^2/cm; the standard, correct unit for coefficient of permeability is actually cm/s (a velocity unit).

q: 315. The ratio of weight of water to the weight of solids is called .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'porosity'; the standard definition of weight of water to weight of solids is actually water content.

q: 316. Valid range for degree of saturations of a soil in percentage .............
explain: Per the reference key this option is marked; the physically valid range for degree of saturation is actually 0 <= S <= 100%.

q: 317. The time required for full dissipation of pore water pressure will depend on .............
options: co-efficient of permeability of soil only
both thickness and co-efficient of permeability only
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'none of the above'; per consolidation theory (Tv = Cv.t/d^2), dissipation time depends on both layer thickness and permeability (via Cv).

q: 318. The maximum water content of a saturated soil at which a reduction in its moisture does not cause a decrease in volume of the soil, is called .............
explain: This is the standard definition of the shrinkage limit, the boundary below which further drying causes no further volume decrease.

q: 319. When water content in a soil is reduced beyond the shrinkage limit, the soil will be in a .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked 'liquid state'; the standard fact is that below the shrinkage limit, soil enters the solid state.

q: 320. The consistency index is given by .............
explain: Consistency index CI = (wL - w)/Ip, comparing liquid limit to natural water content, normalized by plasticity index.

q: 321. The shear failure exhibited by dense sands is known as .............
explain: Dense sands show a distinct peak strength followed by strength drop upon further strain, characteristic of brittle failure.

q: 322. Clays generally exhibit plasticity property when they are mixed with .............
explain: Water is the medium that activates plasticity in clay by allowing particles to slide relative to one another while maintaining cohesion.

q: 323. The shear strength of sands with the following shape will be more .............
explain: Angular, sharp-edged particles interlock more effectively than rounded grains, giving higher shear strength.

q: 324. The ultimate strength of a loose and dense sand samples which are consolidated to the same value of effective stress will be .............
explain: At large strains (critical/ultimate state), both loose and dense sands consolidated to the same effective stress converge to the same ultimate strength.

q: 325. In a consolidated drained test on a normally consolidated clayey soil, the volume of the soil during the shearing will .............
explain: Normally consolidated clay contracts (decreases in volume) during drained shearing, unlike dilative over-consolidated clay.
